SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (epidermis,:
Overview — The Body’s Barrier

The skin is the largest organ — a barrier that also handles thermoregulation, sensation, vitamin D synthesis and immune defence. It has three layers, from surface down:

🔬 Image slot — skin in cross-section — keratinised epidermis, connective-tissue dermis with appendages, and subcutaneous hypodermis
1
Epidermiskeratinised stratified squamous epithelium
2
Dermisconnective tissue + vessels, nerves, appendages
3
Hypodermissubcutaneous adipose tissue
Thick skin (palms/soles) has a very thick epidermis with a stratum lucidum and no hair; thin skin (everywhere else) is thinner, hairy and lacks a lucidum.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — skin — stratified squamous epidermis with a surface keratin layer over a papillary and reticular dermis, with adnexa and subcutaneous fat below
  • Keratinised stratified squamous epidermis at the surface, with a pink keratin (corneum) layer on top.
  • Dermis of connective tissue below, carrying hair follicles, glands, vessels and nerves.
  • Hypodermis of adipose tissue at the base.
Keratinised stratified squamous epidermis over a fibrous dermis with appendages → skin. A stratum lucidum + thick corneum with no hair → thick (palmoplantar) skin.
The Epidermal Layers
🔬 Image slot — epidermis — basale, spinosum, granulosum, (lucidum in thick skin) and corneum, from basement membrane to surface

Deep to superficial — “Come, Let’s Get Sun Burnt” (Basale, Spinosum, Granulosum, Lucidum, Corneum, read bottom-up):

Stratum basale
Single layer of dividing stem cells on the basement membrane; contains melanocytes & Merkel cells
Stratum spinosum
“Prickle cells” joined by desmosomes; contains Langerhans cells
Stratum granulosum
Keratohyalin granules (basophilic) + lamellar granules (lipid waterproofing); cells start to die
Stratum lucidum
A clear layer only in thick (palmoplantar) skin
Stratum corneum
Dead, flattened, anucleate keratin-filled corneocytes — the barrier
Cells are born in the basale and pushed up, dying and keratinising as they go (~28-day turnover; slashed to ~4–7 days in psoriasis). The stratum lucidum is your marker of thick skin.
The Four Epidermal Cell Types
Keratinocytes
The majority; make keratin, migrate up and keratinise
Melanocytes
Neural-crest cells in the basale; make melanin and transfer it to keratinocytes via melanosomes for UV protection
Langerhans cells
Dendritic antigen-presenting cells (bone-marrow-derived) in the spinosum; contain Birbeck granules
Merkel cells
In the basale; mechanoreceptors for fine/sustained touch
Melanocytes make melanin but store it in keratinocytes — the melanin sits like a cap over keratinocyte nuclei to shield DNA from UV. Racial skin-colour differences reflect melanin amount/type, not melanocyte number.
Junctions, the Dermo-Epidermal Junction & Vitamin D
Cell junctions (barrier set)
  • Desmosomes (desmoglein/desmocollin) through the spinosum — mechanical cohesion (target in pemphigus)
  • Tight junctions (claudin-1) in the granulosum — the living water barrier
  • Hemidesmosomes anchor the basale to the basement membrane
Dermo-epidermal junction (BMZ)
  • Lamina lucida → lamina densa (type IV collagen, laminin-332)
  • Hemidesmosomes carry BP180 (type XVII collagen) / BP230 & integrin α6β4
  • Type VII collagen anchoring fibrils tie the lamina densa to the dermis
Split levels map to disease: desmosome → pemphigus; lamina lucida (BP180) → bullous pemphigoid; type VII anchoring fibrils → dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.
Vitamin D: UVB converts epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol → cholecalciferol (D3); the liver 25-hydroxylates and the kidney 1α-hydroxylates it to active calcitriol. Melanin absorbs UVB, so darker skin / high latitudes synthesise less.
Dermis, Hypodermis & Sensory Receptors
🔬 Image slot — dermis — papillary layer with dermal papillae and Meissner corpuscles, reticular layer with Pacinian corpuscles, over subcutaneous fat
Papillary dermis
  • Loose CT; dermal papillae interdigitate with the epidermis
  • Capillaries + Meissner’s corpuscles (light touch)
Reticular dermis
  • Dense irregular CT (collagen + elastic)
  • Appendages + Pacinian corpuscles (pressure/vibration)
  • Hypodermis = adipose tissue for insulation, energy store and cushioning.
  • Receptor summary: Meissner (light touch), Pacinian (pressure/vibration), Merkel (sustained touch), Ruffini (stretch), free nerve endings (pain/temperature).
Meissner = superficial (papillary), light touch; Pacinian = deep, pressure/vibration — an easy pairing to remember.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Basal cell carcinoma
From basal keratinocytes; commonest skin cancer (sun-exposed face); peripheral palisading + stromal clefting; pearly rolled edge (rodent ulcer); rarely metastasises
Squamous cell carcinoma
From keratinocytes; keratin pearls; precursors actinic keratosis → Bowen (in situ); risk ↑ in transplant/immunosuppression (also Marjolin ulcer); can metastasise
Melanoma
Malignant melanocytes (S100/SOX10/Melan-A/HMB-45); ABCDE; superficial-spreading commonest, nodular worst, acral in darker skin; prognosis by Breslow thickness + ulceration (sentinel node); BRAF-targeted therapy
Psoriasis
Parakeratosis, acanthosis, hypogranulosis; Munro microabscesses (corneum) / Kogoj pustules (spinosum); suprapapillary thinning (Auspitz sign); rapid turnover
Pemphigus vs pemphigoid
Pemphigus vulgaris = intra-epidermal, anti-desmoglein 3 (Nikolsky+); bullous pemphigoid = subepidermal (lamina lucida), anti-BP180/BP230 hemidesmosome (tense bullae)
Albinism / vitiligo
Albinism = normal melanocytes but defective melanin synthesis (e.g. tyrosinase); vitiligo = autoimmune melanocyte loss (patchy)
Eczema shows spongiosis (intercellular oedema of the epidermis). Blistering level: pemphigus vulgaris splits intra-epidermally (suprabasal “row of tombstones”, anti-desmoglein 3, Nikolsky+, fish-net IF); bullous pemphigoid splits subepidermally through the lamina lucida (anti-BP180/BP230 hemidesmosome, tense bullae, linear IgG/C3).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Keratinised stratified squamous epidermis + dermis + hypodermis = skin.
Epidermal layers (deep→superficial): basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum.
Stratum lucidum only in thick (palmoplantar) skin.
Four cells: keratinocytes; melanocytes (basale, neural-crest, melanin→keratinocytes); Langerhans (spinosum, antigen-presenting); Merkel (basale, touch).
Melanin protects DNA from UV; melanocyte number is similar across skin colours (melanin amount differs).
Dermis: papillary (Meissner, light touch) + reticular (Pacinian, pressure/vibration).
BCC = basal (pearly, rarely spreads); SCC = keratin pearls; melanoma = melanocytes / Breslow.
Pemphigus = intra-epidermal (desmoglein 3); pemphigoid = subepidermal, lamina lucida (BP180 hemidesmosome).
Split levels: desmosome → pemphigus; lamina lucida BP180 → pemphigoid; type VII → dystrophic EB.
Vitamin D: 7-dehydrocholesterol → D3 (UVB) → liver 25-OH → kidney 1α-OH → calcitriol.
SCC precursors: actinic keratosis → Bowen (in situ) → invasive; melanoma stains S100/SOX10/Melan-A/HMB-45.
SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair Follicle & S:
Overview — The Pilosebaceous Unit

The hair follicle, its sebaceous gland and the arrector pili muscle form the pilosebaceous unit. Follicles and glands are epidermal derivatives that grow down into the dermis; they make hair and sebum.

🔬 Image slot — pilosebaceous unit — hair follicle with its bulb, a sebaceous gland emptying into the follicle, and the arrector pili muscle
  • Sebum lubricates and waterproofs hair and skin and has mild antibacterial action.
  • Glabrous (hairless) skin of the palms and soles has no follicles.
Learn three components: the follicle (makes hair), the sebaceous gland (holocrine, makes sebum) and the arrector pili (smooth muscle, raises the hair).
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — skin section — an oblique hair follicle with concentric root sheaths, a lobulated sebaceous gland opening into it, and an arrector pili muscle
  • A hair follicle — a tubular epithelial structure with concentric root sheaths, often cut obliquely.
  • A lobulated sebaceous gland of pale, foamy (lipid-filled) cells emptying into the follicle.
  • A slip of smooth muscle (arrector pili) running from the follicle to the papillary dermis.
A follicle + a pale foamy sebaceous gland opening into it → pilosebaceous unit. The foamy holocrine cells and central duct name the sebaceous gland.
The Hair Follicle & Hair Bulb
🔬 Image slot — hair bulb — dermal papilla surrounded by the matrix, with the hair shaft (medulla, cortex, cuticle) and inner/outer root sheaths
  • The follicle has an infundibulum (surface to sebaceous duct), an isthmus, and an expanded bulb at the base.
  • The bulb contains the dermal papilla (vascular connective tissue that induces hair growth) surrounded by the proliferating matrix (with melanocytes that colour the hair).
  • Hair shaft layers (inside→out): medulla → cortex (hard/trichocyte keratin, disulphide-cross-linked, formed without keratohyalin, + pigment) → cuticle; fine vellus hairs lack a medulla.
  • Surrounding sheaths: the inner root sheath (three layers outside-in: Henle → Huxley → IRS cuticle, keratinising via trichohyalin granules), the outer root sheath (continuous with the epidermis), a glassy (vitreous) membrane and a connective-tissue sheath.
Dermal papilla = the inducer; matrix = the factory. Matrix melanocytes (replenished from melanocyte stem cells in the bulge) colour the hair; age-related depletion of those bulge stem cells greys it.
The Hair Growth Cycle
1
Anagenactive growth (years); most hairs
2
Catagenbrief regression
3
Telogenrest, then shedding
  • Follicular stem cells live in the “bulge” (at the isthmus, near the arrector pili insertion); they regenerate the follicle each cycle and re-epithelialise the epidermis after burns/wounds. The bulge also holds melanocyte stem cells.
Anagen (grow) → catagen (regress) → telogen (rest) → exogen (shed). On the scalp ~85–90% are anagen, ~1% catagen, ~10–15% telogen (~50–100 hairs/day shed). A stress that pushes many hairs into telogen causes diffuse shedding (telogen effluvium).
The Sebaceous Gland & Arrector Pili
Sebaceous gland
  • Holocrine secretion: cells fill with lipid and disintegrate to release sebum (whole-cell secretion)
  • Empties into the follicle; androgen-driven (enlarges at puberty)
Arrector pili
  • Smooth muscle from the follicle bulge to the papillary dermis
  • Sympathetic contraction → hair erection (“goosebumps”) + sebum expression
  • Some sebaceous glands open directly onto the surface (independent of hair): Meibomian (tarsal) glands of the eyelid, Montgomery glands of the areola, and glands of the lips.
Sebaceous glands are the classic holocrine gland (their modified forms — Meibomian, Zeis, Fordyce, Montgomery — are holocrine too). Contrast with merocrine (eccrine sweat) and apocrine secretion.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Acne vulgaris
Follicular hyperkeratinisation + excess sebum + Cutibacterium acnes + inflammation → comedones, papules, pustules
Androgenetic alopecia
Follicle miniaturisation under DHT (5α-reductase converts T→DHT). Men: minoxidil + finasteride; women (Ludwig pattern): minoxidil ± spironolactone — finasteride is teratogenic, avoid in women of child-bearing potential
Alopecia areata
Autoimmune, non-scarring hair loss (“exclamation-mark” hairs)
Telogen effluvium
Stress/illness pushes many hairs into telogen → diffuse shedding, usually reversible
Sebaceous / pilar cyst
Keratin-filled cyst from the follicle; a “sebaceous cyst” is usually an epidermoid/pilar cyst
Chalazion / stye (hordeolum)
Chalazion = sterile lipogranuloma of a blocked Meibomian gland; stye = acute infection — external (Zeis/Moll) or internal (Meibomian) hordeolum
Hirsutism (androgen-driven terminal hair, e.g. PCOS; vs androgen-independent hypertrichosis) and folliculitis → furuncle → carbuncle (Staph. aureus) are common. Non-scarring alopecia (areata, androgenetic, effluvium) spares the follicular ostia; scarring/cicatricial alopecia (lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus) destroys the bulge → permanent. Severe acne → isotretinoin (highly teratogenic). A recurrent eyelid “chalazion” may be sebaceous carcinoma (biopsy; Muir–Torre).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Pilosebaceous unit = hair follicle + sebaceous gland + arrector pili.
Hair bulb: dermal papilla (inductive) + matrix (proliferation + melanocytes for colour).
Hair shaft inside→out: medulla → cortex → cuticle.
Hair cycle: anagen (grow) → catagen → telogen (rest/shed); stem cells in the bulge.
Sebaceous gland = holocrine (whole-cell → sebum), empties into the follicle, androgen-driven.
Arrector pili = smooth muscle, sympathetic → goosebumps + sebum expression.
Acne = follicular plugging + sebum + C. acnes; Meibomian glands = modified sebaceous (chalazion).
Palms & soles have no hair follicles (glabrous skin).
IRS layers (out→in): Henle → Huxley → IRS cuticle (trichohyalin granules); shaft = hard keratin.
Scarring alopecia destroys the bulge → permanent; non-scarring spares ostia → reversible.
SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat Glands:
Overview — Two Glands for Cooling & Scent

Skin has two kinds of sweat gland, both coiled tubular glands sitting in the dermis:

🔬 Image slot — sweat glands — an eccrine gland opening onto the skin surface and an apocrine gland opening into a hair follicle, both with coiled secretory portions
Eccrine (merocrine)
  • Everywhere; opens onto the skin surface
  • Watery sweat for thermoregulation
Apocrine
  • Axilla, groin, areola, ear; opens into a hair follicle
  • Viscous, odour-producing secretion
Eccrine = surface + cooling; apocrine = follicle + scent. Eccrine glands are the true thermoregulators; apocrine glands switch on at puberty.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — dermal sweat gland — pale secretory coil with clear/dark cells and peripheral myoepithelial cells, alongside a smaller, darker two-layered duct
  • A coiled tubular gland in the deep dermis, cut as clusters of tubules.
  • Secretory coil — larger, paler tubules with myoepithelial cells at the periphery.
  • Duct — smaller, darker (more eosinophilic) tubules with a two-layered (stratified cuboidal) wall.
Pale secretory coil + darker two-layered duct in the dermis → sweat gland. A wide lumen opening into a follicle suggests apocrine; a narrow one opening onto the surface suggests eccrine.
Eccrine (Merocrine) Sweat Glands
  • Widespread (densest on palms, soles, forehead); a simple coiled tubular gland opening directly onto the skin surface via a pore.
  • Secretory coil has clear cells (watery secretion of water & electrolytes), dark cells (glycoprotein) and peripheral myoepithelial cells.
  • The clear cells make an isotonic primary secretion; the water-impermeable duct reabsorbs Na⁺ (via ENaC) & Cl⁻ (via CFTR) faster than water, so the final sweat is hypotonic (ductal Na⁺ reabsorption is ↑ by aldosterone / heat acclimatisation).
  • Secretion is merocrine (exocytosis) and driven by sympathetic cholinergic (ACh) nerves — an exception to the usual adrenergic sympathetic rule.
  • Sweat also carries urea, lactate, ammonia and antimicrobial peptides (dermcidin, cathelicidin) plus IgA — an innate-immune role beyond cooling.
Eccrine sweat cools by evaporation; its duct reclaims salt to leave hypotonic sweat. Uniquely, sympathetic control here is cholinergic.
Apocrine Sweat Glands
🔬 Image slot — apocrine gland — wide-lumen secretory coil with apical 'blebbing' cells and myoepithelial cells, opening into a hair follicle
  • Restricted to the axilla, areola, genital/perianal skin, external ear (ceruminous) and eyelid (Moll); present from fetal life but become active at puberty (androgen-dependent).
  • Large lumen; secretory cells release a viscous, protein/lipid-rich fluid; they empty into the hair follicle, not the surface.
  • Secretion itself is odourless — body odour arises when skin bacteria break it down.
  • Controlled by sympathetic adrenergic nerves.
  • Despite the name, human apocrine sweat glands secrete largely by merocrine exocytosis; true apocrine (decapitation) secretion is exemplified by the lactating mammary gland.
Ceruminous and Moll (eyelid) glands are modified apocrine. Cerumen (earwax) = ceruminous (apocrine) secretion + sebaceous secretion + shed cells. Apocrine sweat is scent-related, not thermoregulatory.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cystic fibrosis sweat test
High sweat chloride (normally CFTR reabsorbs duct Cl⁻; loss raises Cl⁻ & Na⁺). Pilocarpine iontophoresis; ≥60 mmol/L diagnostic (30–59 intermediate). “Salty baby”, hyponatraemic dehydration
Hyperhidrosis
Excess eccrine sweating (primary focal palmar/axillary vs secondary generalised). Ladder: aluminium chloride → iontophoresis → botulinum toxin (blocks ACh) → sympathectomy (risk: compensatory sweating)
Hidradenitis suppurativa
Follicular occlusion disease (apocrine involvement secondary) of intertriginous apocrine-bearing skin (axillae/groin) → painful nodules, sinus tracts, scarring
Miliaria (heat rash)
Blocked eccrine ducts trap sweat — crystallina (superficial, clear, non-itchy), rubra (itchy “prickly heat”), profunda (deep)
Cerumen impaction
Earwax from ceruminous (modified apocrine) glands blocking the ear canal
Anhidrosis
Heat intolerance from absent glands (ectodermal dysplasia) or acquired causes: anticholinergic drugs, diabetic autonomic neuropathy
Bromhidrosis (body odour) is bacterial breakdown of apocrine secretion (chromhidrosis = coloured sweat); Fox–Fordyce = apocrine duct obstruction. Frey syndrome: gustatory facial sweating after parotid surgery (aberrant auriculotemporal cholinergic reinnervation; Minor starch–iodine test). Because eccrine control is cholinergic, anticholinergics impair sweating (heat risk).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Eccrine (merocrine) = widespread, opens on the surface, watery thermoregulatory sweat, cholinergic sympathetic.
Apocrine = axilla/groin/areola/ear, opens into a hair follicle, viscous/odorous, adrenergic, starts at puberty.
Eccrine secretory coil: clear cells (water) + dark cells (glycoprotein) + myoepithelial cells.
The duct reabsorbs NaCl → hypotonic sweat.
Cystic fibrosis → high sweat chloride (CFTR duct can’t reabsorb Cl⁻) — the sweat test.
Ceruminous (earwax) & Moll (eyelid) glands are modified apocrine.
Hidradenitis suppurativa = apocrine gland disease (axilla/groin).
Hyperhidrosis treated with botulinum toxin (blocks ACh); apocrine odour needs bacterial action.
“Apocrine” is a misnomer — these glands secrete mostly by merocrine exocytosis; the mammary gland is the true decapitation-apocrine.
Duct reabsorbs Na⁺ via ENaC + Cl⁻ via CFTR (isotonic → hypotonic); sweat carries dermcidin (antimicrobial).
SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (retina, corn:
Overview — Three Tunics

The eye is built from three concentric coats that refract light onto the retina, where it is transduced into nerve signals sent down the optic nerve.

🔬 Image slot — eye in cross-section — fibrous coat (cornea/sclera), vascular uvea (choroid, ciliary body, iris), and neural retina, with the lens behind the iris
1
Fibrous coatsclera + transparent cornea
2
Vascular coat (uvea)choroid, ciliary body, iris
3
Neural coatthe retina
Three structures do the optical work: the cornea (main refraction), the lens (fine focus/accommodation) and the retina (phototransduction).
Embryology ties it together: neuroectoderm (optic cup) → neural retina + RPE (their potential space is where the retina detaches); surface ectoderm → lens + corneal epithelium; neural crest → corneal stroma/endothelium, sclera & ciliary muscle.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — ocular tissues — the layered avascular cornea, the multilayered retina with its pigment epithelium, and the anucleate fibre-filled lens
  • Cornea — a transparent, avascular 5-layered structure with a squamous surface epithelium.
  • Retina — a distinctly multilayered neural sheet with a pigmented layer (RPE) at its outer edge.
  • Lens — an avascular mass of elongated lens fibres under a thick capsule.
A layered avascular cornea, a multilayered pigmented retina, or a fibre-filled lens → eye. Count the layers to name the tissue.
The Cornea — Five Layers
🔬 Image slot — cornea — epithelium, Bowman's layer, stroma (regular collagen lamellae), Descemet's membrane, and endothelium
1. Epithelium
Non-keratinised stratified squamous; regenerates from limbal stem cells
2. Bowman’s layer
Acellular condensed collagen; does not regenerate (scars)
3. Stroma
~90% of thickness; regularly arranged collagen lamellae + keratocytes → transparency
4. Descemet’s membrane
Thick basement membrane of the endothelium
5. Endothelium
Single layer that pumps water out to keep the cornea clear; does not regenerate
The cornea is avascular (fed by tears & aqueous). Transparency depends on the regular collagen spacing and the endothelial pump; endothelial loss (e.g. Fuchs’ dystrophy) causes corneal oedema. A pre-Descemet’s (Dua’s) layer is now also described; loss of limbal stem cells (burns, Stevens–Johnson) causes conjunctivalisation.
The Retina — Photoreceptors & the “Inverted” Layers
🔬 Image slot — retina — RPE, photoreceptor rods/cones, outer & inner nuclear layers, bipolar and ganglion cells, and the nerve fibre layer
  • The retina is “inverted”: light passes through the inner layers to reach the photoreceptors at the back.
  • Signal path: photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell → optic nerve, modulated laterally by horizontal (outer plexiform) and amacrine (inner plexiform) interneurons — the two plexiform layers are the synaptic layers.
  • Rods = dim/night vision (rhodopsin), peripheral; cones = colour (three opsins — S/M/L blue/green/red) & high acuity, concentrated at the fovea.
  • Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) — phagocytoses shed photoreceptor discs, regenerates vitamin A (visual cycle), and forms the outer blood-retinal barrier (the inner BRB is the retinal capillary endothelium).
Fovea = cones only, highest acuity (an avascular pit); the optic disc = blind spot (axons exit, no photoreceptors). Muller cells are the retinal glia.
Phototransduction & the Ten Layers
The “dark current” (counter-intuitive): in the dark photoreceptors are depolarised and tonically release glutamate. Light isomerises 11-cis → all-trans retinal in rhodopsin → transducin → cGMP falls → cation channels close → the cell hyperpolarises and releases less glutamate.
  • Ten layers (outer→inner): RPE, photoreceptor segments, outer limiting membrane, outer nuclear, outer plexiform (synapse), inner nuclear (bipolar/horizontal/amacrine/Müller), inner plexiform (synapse), ganglion cell, nerve fibre, inner limiting membrane.
  • The avascular outer retina is fed by the choriocapillaris across Bruch’s membrane — the site where drusen accumulate in AMD.
The Lens, Accommodation & Aqueous
Lens
  • Avascular, biconvex; capsule (thick BM), anterior epithelium, and lens fibres (lose organelles, packed with crystallins)
  • Suspended by zonular fibres from the ciliary body
Accommodation
  • Ciliary muscle contracts → zonules relax → lens rounds up for near vision
  • Ciliary body: its non-pigmented ciliary epithelium secretes aqueous humour (carbonic-anhydrase-dependent — target of acetazolamide/dorzolamide) and houses the ciliary muscle (parasympathetic, CN III); the iris has sphincter (parasympathetic, constricts) and dilator (sympathetic) muscles.
  • Aqueous: ciliary body → posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork & canal of Schlemm. Blocked drainage → raised pressure (glaucoma).
Lens fibres are packed with crystallins and lose their organelles for transparency — opacification of these proteins is a cataract.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cataract
Opacification of lens crystallins — nuclear, cortical, posterior subcapsular (steroids/diabetes). Painless progressive loss; treated by phacoemulsification + IOL
Glaucoma
Progressive optic neuropathy with disc cupping. Open-angle = trabecular outflow resistance (chronic, painless, commonest); angle-closure = acute painful red eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil (emergency); IOP not always raised (normal-tension)
Age-related macular degeneration
Dry = drusen (at Bruch’s membrane) + geographic atrophy; wet = choroidal neovascularisation (metamorphopsia) treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF → central vision loss
Diabetic retinopathy
Non-proliferative (microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool spots) vs proliferative (neovascularisation); maculopathy is the main cause of visual loss (inner blood-retinal barrier breakdown)
Retinal detachment
Neural retina separates from RPE → sudden “curtain”/field loss. Rhegmatogenous (tear; flashes & floaters; emergency), tractional (PDR), exudative
Fuchs’ endothelial dystrophy
Loss of corneal endothelial cells → corneal oedema & cloudiness
Retinitis pigmentosa = progressive rod degeneration (night blindness, tunnel vision). Retinoblastoma (childhood) — leukocoria (white red reflex), Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes (vs neuroblastoma’s lumen-less Homer–Wright), RB1 gene. Also: vitamin A deficiency → xerophthalmia/Bitot spots; CRAO → cherry-red spot; HSV dendritic ulcer (steroids contraindicated); presbyopia = age-related lens hardening.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Three tunics: fibrous (sclera/cornea) → vascular uvea (choroid, ciliary body, iris) → neural retina.
Cornea = 5 layers (epithelium, Bowman’s, stroma, Descemet’s, endothelium); avascular; endothelium pumps water & does not regenerate.
Retina is inverted; signal = photoreceptor → bipolar → ganglion → optic nerve.
Rods = dim/night (rhodopsin); cones = colour/acuity (fovea = cones only).
RPE phagocytoses discs, stores vitamin A, forms the blood-retinal barrier; optic disc = blind spot.
Lens = avascular crystallin-filled fibres; accommodation = ciliary muscle contracts → zonules relax → lens rounds.
Aqueous: ciliary body → canal of Schlemm; blocked drainage → glaucoma (raised IOP, disc cupping).
Cataract = lens opacity; macular degeneration = drusen/RPE; Fuchs’ = corneal endothelial loss.
Dark current: photoreceptors are depolarised in the dark (release glutamate) and hyperpolarise to light.
Glaucoma: open-angle (chronic, commonest) vs angle-closure (acute emergency); wet AMD → anti-VEGF.
SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (cochlea, org:
Overview — Three Parts, Two Senses

The ear handles hearing and balance. It has three parts, and the inner ear splits into a hearing organ (cochlea) and a balance organ (vestibular apparatus).

🔬 Image slot — ear overview — external (pinna, canal, tympanic membrane), middle (ossicles), and inner ear (cochlea + vestibular labyrinth)
1
External earpinna, canal, tympanic membrane — collects sound
2
Middle earair-filled; ossicles amplify & transmit
3
Inner earcochlea (hearing) + vestibular (balance)
Sound is converted to a neural signal in the organ of Corti (cochlea); head position/movement is sensed by the vestibular apparatus. Both use hair cells.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — cochlea in cross-section — the spiral with scala vestibuli, scala media containing the organ of Corti, and scala tympani
  • A spiral (cochlea) cut through several turns, each turn showing three fluid chambers.
  • The organ of Corti sitting on the basilar membrane in the middle chamber (scala media).
  • Elastic cartilage (pinna), ossicles/bone, or the sensory epithelia of the vestibule elsewhere.
A bony spiral with three chambers and a hair-cell organ on the basilar membrane → cochlea/organ of Corti.
External & Middle Ear
External ear
  • Pinna = elastic cartilage + skin
  • Canal: skin with ceruminous (wax) & sebaceous glands and hairs
  • Tympanic membrane: outer squamous, middle fibrous, inner cuboidal
Middle ear
  • Air-filled cavity; ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify & transmit
  • Eustachian tube to the nasopharynx equalises pressure
  • Stapes footplate vibrates the oval window
Ceruminous glands are modified apocrine glands making earwax; the ossicles amplify sound to overcome the impedance of inner-ear fluid.
The Cochlea & Organ of Corti (High-Yield)
🔬 Image slot — organ of Corti — inner & outer hair cells with stereocilia on the basilar membrane, overlaid by the tectorial membrane, with supporting cells and the tunnel of Corti
  • Three chambers: scala vestibuli (perilymph) → scala media / cochlear duct (endolymph, high K⁺) → scala tympani (perilymph). Reissner’s membrane roofs the scala media; the helicotrema joins vestibuli & tympani at the apex; the round window relieves pressure.
  • The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane: inner hair cells (~1 row; the main sensory cells — ~95% of afferent CN VIII fibres) and outer hair cells (~3 rows; amplify via prestin electromotility, mostly efferent input), plus pillar cells (tunnel of Corti) and Deiters supporting cells.
  • Sound → basilar membrane vibrates → stereocilia deflect (outer hair cell tips are embedded in the tectorial membrane; inner hair cells are bent by endolymph shear) → tip links open MET channels → K⁺ enters from endolymph → depolarisation → cochlear nerve (CN VIII).
Tonotopy: the stiff narrow base detects high frequencies; the floppy wide apex detects low frequencies. The stria vascularis secretes K⁺-rich endolymph and generates the +80 mV endocochlear potential that drives transduction; outer-hair-cell electromotility produces otoacoustic emissions (used in newborn screening). Afferents arise from the spiral ganglion in the modiolus.
The Vestibular Apparatus (Balance)
🔬 Image slot — vestibular sensors — maculae of utricle/saccule with otoliths on the otolithic membrane, and cristae ampullares of the semicircular canals with cupula
Maculae (utricle & saccule)
  • Detect linear acceleration & gravity (utricle horizontal, saccule vertical)
  • Hair cells under an otolithic membrane with otoliths (calcium carbonate/calcite); polarity reverses at the striola
Cristae (semicircular canals)
  • Detect angular (rotational) acceleration
  • Hair cells in a cupula within the ampulla
Vestibular hair cells have stereocilia + a single kinocilium; bending toward the kinocilium depolarises them. Type I (flask-shaped, calyx ending) and type II (cylindrical). Signals travel via the vestibular nerve (CN VIII).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Conductive hearing loss
External/middle ear: wax, otitis media (acute vs effusion/“glue ear” vs chronic suppurative), perforation, or otosclerosis (AD stapes fixation; Carhart notch; stapedectomy)
Sensorineural hearing loss
Cochlea/CN VIII: presbycusis, noise-induced (4 kHz notch), ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides & cisplatin = irreversible; loop diuretics, high-dose aspirin/quinine = reversible). Aids / cochlear implants
Presbycusis / noise damage
Outer hair cells at the base lost first → high-frequency hearing loss
Ménière’s disease
Endolymphatic hydrops → episodic vertigo, tinnitus, aural fullness & fluctuating low-frequency SNHL; salt restriction + betahistine
BPPV
Displaced otoliths in the (usually posterior) semicircular canal → brief positional vertigo; Dix–Hallpike diagnoses, Epley treats
Cholesteatoma
Keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear (congenital or acquired via pars flaccida retraction; not a neoplasm) → erosion of ossicles/facial nerve/lateral SCC; surgical
Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) at the cerebellopontine angle causes unilateral SNHL & tinnitus (bilateral → NF2; MRI IAM). Rinne: AC>BC normal, BC>AC (“negative”) = conductive. Weber lateralises to a conductive ear, away from a sensorineural ear. Vestibular neuritis = vertigo, no hearing loss; labyrinthitis adds hearing loss.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Organ of Corti (on the basilar membrane, scala media) = the hearing sensory organ.
Inner hair cells = main sensory (afferent); outer hair cells = amplify (lost first in presbycusis/noise).
Endolymph (high K⁺, scala media, from the stria vascularis) vs perilymph (high Na⁺).
Tonotopy: base = high frequency, apex = low frequency.
Vestibular: maculae (utricle/saccule, otoliths → linear/gravity); cristae (semicircular canals, cupula → angular).
Ossicles amplify; Eustachian tube equalises pressure; ceruminous glands = modified apocrine (wax).
Conductive (external/middle: wax, otitis media, otosclerosis) vs sensorineural (cochlea/CN VIII).
Ménière’s = endolymphatic hydrops; cholesteatoma = keratinising squamous in the middle ear.
Transduction: tip links open MET channels, K⁺ from endolymph depolarises hair cells (endocochlear potential +80 mV).
Outer hair cells amplify via prestin → otoacoustic emissions (newborn screen); Reissner’s membrane roofs the scala media.
SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfactory Epithel:
Overview — The Sense of Smell

The olfactory epithelium detects odorants and is the sensory sheet for smell. It sits in the roof of the nasal cavity (superior concha & adjacent septum) and is a specialised pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

🔬 Image slot — olfactory epithelium — tall pseudostratified epithelium with olfactory neurons, sustentacular and basal cells, over a lamina propria with Bowman's glands and nerve bundles
  • Its receptor cells are true neurons whose axons form cranial nerve I (olfactory).
  • Uniquely, these neurons are continuously replaced throughout life.
It resembles respiratory epithelium but is taller, has no goblet cells, and carries Bowman’s glands and olfactory nerve bundles in its lamina propria.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — olfactory mucosa — a thick pseudostratified epithelium with an apical layer of olfactory cilia, over serous Bowman's glands and unmyelinated nerve bundles
  • A tall pseudostratified columnar epithelium, thicker than respiratory epithelium, with no goblet cells.
  • An apical layer of olfactory cilia (non-motile) forming a surface mat.
  • Bowman’s (olfactory) glands — serous glands — and bundles of unmyelinated axons in the lamina propria.
Tall pseudostratified epithelium with no goblet cells + Bowman’s glands & nerve bundles beneath → olfactory epithelium. The absence of goblet cells separates it from respiratory epithelium.
The Three Cell Types (+ Bowman’s Glands)
Olfactory receptor neurons
Bipolar neurons; a dendrite ends in an olfactory knob bearing non-motile cilia (odorant receptors); the axon runs to CN I. The only neurons directly exposed to the environment
Sustentacular (supporting) cells
Tall columnar cells with apical microvilli that support and insulate the neurons
Basal cells
Stem cells — horizontal (quiescent reserve) & globose (active progenitors) — that regenerate the receptor neurons and sustentacular cells
Bowman’s glands
Serous glands in the lamina propria whose secretion dissolves odorants and keeps the surface moist
Neuron (senses) + sustentacular (supports) + basal (regenerates). Bowman’s glands provide the serous fluid (with odorant-binding proteins) in which odorants dissolve; the unmyelinated axons are wrapped by olfactory ensheathing cells (a special glia enabling lifelong regrowth).
How Smell Works & Neuronal Regeneration
1
Odorant dissolves & bindsto receptors on the olfactory cilia
2
G-protein / cAMP cascadedepolarises the neuron
3
Axons pierce the cribriform plate→ olfactory bulb (CN I)
  • In the bulb, axons synapse in glomeruli with mitral & tufted cells (granule cells give lateral inhibition) → olfactory tract → cortex.
  • One neuron–one receptor: each neuron expresses just one of ~400 odorant-receptor genes (GPCRs), and like-receptor axons converge on the same glomerulus — odours are read as a combinatorial pattern.
  • Smell reaches the primary (piriform) olfactory cortex, amygdala & entorhinal cortex without an obligatory thalamic relay (hence its strong memory/emotion links); conscious odour discrimination does use a mediodorsal-thalamus → orbitofrontal route.
  • Olfactory neurons regenerate from basal cells throughout life — one of the few sites of adult neurogenesis.
The olfactory cilia are non-motile (bearing receptors) — unlike the motile cilia of respiratory epithelium. Transduction: odorant → receptor → Golf → adenylyl cyclase III → cAMP → CNG cation channel (Ca2+ in) → Ca2+-activated Cl⁻ efflux amplifies the depolarisation.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Anosmia — trauma
Head injury shearing the olfactory nerves at the cribriform plate → loss of smell
Anosmia — viral / obstructive
URTI/COVID-19 (infects ACE2⁺ sustentacular cells; neurons spared → usually reversible), nasal polyps or congestion
Neurodegeneration
Early anosmia in Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease
Kallmann syndrome
Anosmia + hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (X-linked KAL1/anosmin-1; GnRH neurons fail to migrate from the olfactory placode; absent olfactory bulbs on MRI)
Esthesioneuroblastoma
Olfactory neuroblastoma (nasal vault); Homer-Wright rosettes, dumbbell mass eroding the cribriform plate; Hyams grade / Kadish stage
CSF rhinorrhoea
Cribriform-plate fracture can leak CSF into the nose (and risk meningitis)
Loss of smell is often an early clue (COVID-19; before the motor signs of Parkinson’s). Terms: anosmia (absent), hyposmia (reduced), parosmia (distorted — a sign of regrowth), phantosmia (no stimulus). Test each nostril with a non-irritant odour (coffee) — not ammonia, which stimulates trigeminal CN V and fools an anosmic.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Tall pseudostratified columnar, no goblet cells, Bowman’s glands + nerve bundles beneath = olfactory epithelium.
Three cells: olfactory receptor neurons (bipolar, non-motile cilia, axon → CN I); sustentacular (support); basal (stem).
Olfactory neurons are the only neurons directly exposed to the environment and regenerate from basal cells (adult neurogenesis).
Bowman’s glands (serous) dissolve odorants.
Axons pierce the cribriform plate → olfactory bulb; smell bypasses the thalamus.
Olfactory cilia are non-motile (unlike respiratory motile cilia).
Anosmia: cribriform trauma, viral (COVID-19), early Parkinson’s/Alzheimer’s.
Kallmann syndrome = anosmia + hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
One neuron–one receptor (of ~400 GPCRs); like-receptor axons converge on one glomerulus (combinatorial coding).
Cascade: odorant → Golf → AC III → cAMP → CNG channel → Ca2+-activated Cl⁻ efflux.
Test smell with a non-irritant (coffee), not ammonia (CN V); parosmia signals regrowth.
SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste Buds:
Overview — The Sense of Taste

Taste buds are the chemoreceptor organs of gustation. They are barrel-shaped clusters of cells set within the stratified squamous epithelium of the tongue papillae (and soft palate, epiglottis and pharynx), opening at the surface via a taste pore.

🔬 Image slot — taste bud — a barrel-shaped cluster of taste cells within the epithelium, opening at a taste pore, with microvilli projecting into it
  • They detect the five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
  • Taste combines with smell to give the perception of flavour.
Taste buds sit on fungiform, circumvallate and foliate papillae — but not on the numerous keratinised filiform papillae.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — tongue epithelium — a pale, oval, barrel-shaped taste bud spanning the epithelium with an apical taste pore, on a papilla
  • A pale, oval (barrel-shaped) cluster of cells spanning the epithelial thickness.
  • An apical taste pore with microvilli (“gustatory hairs”) projecting into it.
  • Located on a papilla; a deep surrounding trench with serous glands indicates a circumvallate papilla.
A pale barrel-shaped intra-epithelial cluster opening at a taste pore → taste bud. Name the papilla by its shape and the presence of a moat/glands.
The Tongue Papillae
Filiform
Most numerous, keratinised, pointed; NO taste buds (provide a rough gripping surface)
Fungiform
Mushroom-shaped, on the anterior tongue; a few taste buds on the top
Circumvallate (vallate)
Large, ~8–12 in a V at the back, each in a moat/trench; many taste buds; flushed by von Ebner’s (serous) glands
Foliate
Leaf-like folds on the lateral tongue; taste buds prominent in children (regress in adults)
Filiform = no taste buds; circumvallate = most taste buds + von Ebner’s glands. Von Ebner’s glands flush the trench so new tastants can be sampled.
Taste-Bud Cells & What They Sense
Type I (support)
Most numerous, glial-like: GLAST glutamate uptake, NTPDase2 clears ATP, K⁺ buffering; a proposed role in amiloride-sensitive (ENaC) salt
Type II (receptor)
Detect sweet, bitter & umami via GPCRs (T1R/T2R) coupled to gustducin; release ATP through CALHM1 channels (no classic synapse)
Type III (presynaptic)
Detect sour via the OTOP1 proton channel (marker PKD2L1); form a true synapse with the sensory nerve
Basal cells
Stem cells that regenerate the taste cells (turnover ~10–14 days)
Type II = sweet/bitter/umami (GPCR); Type III = sour (synapse); Type I = salt/support. Taste cells are epithelial (not neurons) and are constantly renewed by basal cells.
Taste Transduction & Nerve Supply
🔬 Image slot — taste innervation map — anterior two-thirds via CN VII (chorda tympani), posterior third via CN IX, epiglottis/pharynx via CN X, to the nucleus solitarius
  • Tastants dissolve in saliva → enter the taste pore → act on the microvilli: salt (ENaC Na⁺ channel), sour (H⁺ via OTOP1), sweet/bitter/umami (GPCRs → gustducin).
●
Anterior 2/3 tongueCN VII (facial, via chorda tympani)
●
Posterior 1/3 tongueCN IX (glossopharyngeal)
●
Epiglottis / pharynxCN X (vagus)
First-order cell bodies sit in the geniculate (VII), petrosal/inferior (IX) and nodose/inferior (X) ganglia. All taste fibres converge on the rostral nucleus of the solitary tract → ipsilateral VPM thalamus → gustatory cortex (insula / frontal operculum).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Ageusia / dysgeusia
Loss/alteration of taste — drugs, zinc deficiency, chemo/radiotherapy, viral (COVID-19)
Facial nerve (VII) lesions
Bell’s palsy can affect the chorda tympani → loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Loss of flavour
Anosmia markedly reduces flavour, as flavour = taste + smell
Geographic tongue
Benign migratory loss of filiform papillae → map-like red patches
Ageing
Reduced taste-bud number/regeneration → blunted taste in the elderly
Radiotherapy
Damages taste cells & salivary flow → taste disturbance (often partly recovers)
Because taste cells regenerate from basal cells, many taste disturbances (post-viral, post-radiotherapy) partially recover over time.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Taste buds = barrel-shaped intra-epithelial clusters opening at a taste pore.
Filiform papillae = keratinised, NO taste buds (most numerous); circumvallate = most taste buds + von Ebner’s serous glands.
Cells: type II (sweet/bitter/umami, GPCR), type III (sour, synapse), type I (salt/support), basal (stem).
Five tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami; salt via Na⁺ channels, sour via H⁺, the rest via GPCRs.
Nerves: anterior 2/3 = CN VII (chorda tympani); posterior 1/3 = CN IX; epiglottis = CN X.
All taste afferents → nucleus solitarius → thalamus → gustatory cortex.
Taste cells regenerate (~10–14 days) from basal cells.
Ageusia: zinc deficiency, drugs, COVID-19; flavour = taste + smell.
Molecules: sour = OTOP1 (PKD2L1 cells); sweet/bitter/umami GPCRs → gustducin; Type II ATP via CALHM1; salt = ENaC.
Ganglia: geniculate (VII), petrosal (IX), nodose (X); taste is ipsilateral → insular cortex.
